bootstrap.php
<?php

define('BASE_PATH', __DIR__);
require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

use function Naf\app;

app()->run();
public/index.php
<?php

require dirname(__DIR__) . '/bootstrap.php';
app/routes.php
<?php

use function Naf\{json, route};

route()->add('GET', '/', fn() => json(['ok' => true]), 'home');
.env
APP_ENV=dev

php -S 127.0.0.1:8000 -t public

In another terminal, curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/ should return {"ok": true} (with whitespace for readability). This path needs no view, form, session or database plugin. For a complete application using this structure, continue with the JSON API without a database. Follow that tutorial in its own directory; it includes its own bootstrap, routes and Composer file.

docs.title: Starter versions and updates
docs.text:
These notes are for checking an existing project or choosing dependency updates. A fresh starter installation can proceed directly to Your first application.

Starter 0.2.5 requires and locks framework 0.2.12, form 0.2.4, session 0.2.3 and view 0.2.3 (with Nyholm PSR-7 1.8.2). Its minimum constraints retain the framework, form and view fixes even with the lowest dependency resolution. Fresh create-project installations work with their committed lock file; no follow-up update is needed.

The starter no longer requires PDO. Framework supplies HEAD fallback, automatic OPTIONS, 405 responses with Allow and the optional handle() request API; app()->run() remains unchanged. Form checks every unsafe method and provides csrf()->token(); framework guards work under CLI and header listeners compose. The package overview lists releases.

Versions included in starter 0.2.4

Starter 0.2.4 locks Framework 0.2.9, Form 0.2.4, Session 0.2.3 and View 0.2.3. Its framework dependency requires PDO. Use the update command below to adopt the current framework; the normal bootstrap remains app()->run().

Versions included in starters 0.2.2 and 0.2.3

Starters 0.2.2 and 0.2.3 ship the same working dependency lock: framework 0.2.3, form 0.2.2, session 0.2.1 and view 0.2.1. They exclude Nyholm PSR-7 below 1.8.2 to avoid PHP 8.4+ deprecation errors. The welcome page, /contact form and POST /api demonstration work directly after installation; no extra Composer update or response listener is needed. Starter 0.2.3 adds the interactive welcome page and Start fresh guidance; its dependencies are unchanged.

For an application created from an older starter, update the required minimum versions:

composer require 'naf/framework:^0.2.12' 'naf/form:^0.2.4' 'naf/view:^0.2.3' --with-all-dependencies

To move a new or existing project to the current compatible releases, run composer update and test your application before deploying it. Commit composer.lock; deployments should use composer install to reproduce that tested dependency set. Review the Framework 0.2.12 migration notes when updating an older framework.

docs.title: Environment and next steps
docs.text:
Use APP_ENV=dev locally, APP_ENV=test for tests and APP_ENV=prod in production. Use these exact values: production is not the production constant. Keep .env and .env.local out of version control. See Configuration.

  • Your first application — a website and a JSON endpoint.
  • Application scenarios — complete small projects, from two HTML pages to a storage-free JSON API.
  • Choosing packages — add only what your application needs.
  • Requests and responses — read incoming data and return a response.

docs.title: Application lifecycle
docs.text: The first app() call boots NAF. app()->run() then handles the HTTP request. Existing applications continue to use this bootstrap. Framework 0.2.12+ also provides handle() for a supplied PSR-7 request; adopting it is optional. This order determines where to register services, routes and listeners.

docs.title: Application boot
docs.text:
In the starter, public/index.php requires root bootstrap.php. The bootstrap defines BASE_PATH, loads Composer, registers application services and calls app()->run().

The first app() creates App with AutoResolvingContainer(new Container()). Boot:

  1. Loads .env.local if present, otherwise .env.
  2. Registers core services, including configuration, routing, events, logging and errors.
  3. Discovers installed Composer packages with type naf-plugin and registers all plugins.
  4. Resolves plugin order, then loads each plugin's routes and helpers before its bootstrap.
  5. Loads application routes and registers core guard rules, including under CLI since Framework 0.2.9.

Configuration is resolved lazily and merged in core, plugin, application order. Application values win. See Configuration and Plugin order.

docs.title: Code locations and timing
HTTP handling
docs.text:
During run(), NAF:

  1. Creates the PSR-7 server request and passes it to handle() (Framework 0.2.12+).
  2. Dispatches request.start and matches an HTTP method and path.
  3. Constructs a controller through the default container, or selects a closure.
  4. Dispatches controller.calling and invokes the handler with named route parameters.
  5. Receives a PSR-7 response and dispatches controller.called.
  6. Normalizes content rules and finalizes the response, then emits status, headers and body.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant I as index.php
    participant A as NAF
    participant R as Router
    participant C as Controller
    B->>I: GET /hello/Ada
    I->>A: bootstrap.php: app()
    Note over A: boot: .env, services,<br/>plugins, routes, guards
    I->>A: run()
    A->>A: request.start
    A->>R: match GET /hello/Ada
    R-->>A: handler, name = Ada
    A->>A: controller.calling (CSRF)
    A->>C: hello(name: "Ada")
    C-->>A: response
    A->>A: controller.called, response.send
    A->>A: response.header
    A-->>B: status, headers, body

After sending headers, NAF dispatches response.body before writing the body, then response.end afterwards. An exception during request handling enters the error path: an exception listener may return a response, otherwise the error handler renders one.

Routing and controller exceptions enter the error path. An exception listener can return a response; otherwise the error handler renders one. Normal emission terminates the request. Controllers return responses rather than echoing output or sending headers.

See Events for payloads and replacement behavior. To change headers, return a new response from response.header. A response returned from controller.called or response.send does not replace the emitted response.

docs.title: Handle a supplied request
docs.text:
Framework 0.2.12+ provides App::handle(ServerRequestInterface $request): ResponseInterface. It replaces request and parameter bindings, clears the matched route, runs request/controller events, converts exceptions through the normal error path, normalizes content rules and dispatches response.send during finalization. It returns without emitting headers, writing output or exiting. See the complete request test.

The emitter owns response.header, response.body and response.end; handle() does not run them. Keep real HTTP tests for emitted cookies, headers, streams and SAPI behavior. app()->run() creates the server request, delegates handling and emits the response.

Sequential calls share application and plugin services. Keep request-specific state out of shared services; this API alone does not guarantee isolation for persistent HTTP workers. Concurrent or reentrant handling on one App throws LogicException.

docs.title: CLI and workers
docs.text:
Under CLI, app()->run() returns without routing or emitting HTTP. Commands still use application boot, services and configuration. Use handle() for request tests without emission, and a running HTTP application to verify the emitted response. Framework 0.2.9+ also registers the core guard rules under CLI, so View rendering and HTML escaping work in commands and workers after boot.

Workers can process many jobs in one process. Shared services and plugin state can survive between jobs; do not keep request identities or mutable job data in shared services. Bound worker lifetimes and restart them after deployments. See Queues and Testing.

docs.title: Sending mail
docs.text:
naf/mail builds messages and delivers them through a transport. The default transport uses PHP's mail() and requires a configured delivery system. In local development, first select the shipped capture transport or the contact form outbox.

Use a queue when delivery should occur after the HTTP response. A successful transport call does not prove that a recipient received the message.

Required packages

In an existing NAF application:

composer require naf/mail

docs.title: Sending a message
docs.text:
mail() creates a message with configured sender defaults, and mailer() sends it. Both are imported from Naf\Mail.

use function Naf\Mail\{mail, mailer};

$message = mail()
    ->setFrom('hello@example.com')
    ->addTo('john@example.com')
    ->setSubject('Hello from NAF')
    ->setContent('<b>Welcome!</b>');

mailer()->send($message);

Every setter returns the message, so the calls chain in any order you like.

docs.title: Recipients
docs.text:
mail()
    ->addTo('john@example.com')
    ->addTo('jane@example.com')     // call it again for a second recipient
    ->addCc('archive@example.com')
    ->addBcc('audit@example.com')
    ->setFrom('hello@example.com')
    ->setReplyTo('support@example.com');

addTo, addCc and addBcc append; setFrom and setReplyTo replace. There is no method to remove a recipient — build the message with the ones you want.

docs.title: HTML or plain text
docs.text:
setContent() treats its argument as HTML unless you say otherwise:

->setContent('<b>Welcome!</b>')          // HTML
->setContent('Welcome!', false)          // plain text

With naf/mail 0.2.3+, add a text alternative to an HTML message:

->setContent('<b>Welcome!</b>')
->setTextContent('Welcome!')

Both built-in delivery transports send these as multipart/alternative. With setContent($body, false), the main body is plain text and a text alternative is ignored. getTextContent() returns the supplied alternative or null.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
->addAttachment('report.pdf', '/path/to/report.pdf');

The first argument is the filename the recipient sees, the second the file on disk. A third argument marks the attachment as inline, which is how you reference an image from the HTML body:

mail()
    ->addAttachment('logo.png', '/path/to/logo.png', true)
    ->setContent('<img src="cid:logo.png">');

The cid: reference uses the name you gave, not the path.

docs.title: Delivery failures
docs.text:
send() returns bool. The PHP-mail transport throws Naf\Mail\Exceptions\MailException when PHP's mail() refuses the message. The SMTP transport wraps connection and delivery failures in the same exception, preserving the cause.

use Naf\Mail\Exceptions\MailException;
use function Naf\Mail\mailer;

try {
    mailer()->send($message);
} catch (MailException $e) {
    // log it, queue a retry, tell somebody
}

Checking the return value alone will not catch an exception. Custom transports, or a cancelled SMTP send, may return false; callers that accept either should handle both.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Key Type Default Effect mail:transport class name Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\MailTransport Transport used by the shared mailer(); the class must implement TransportInterface mail:from string empty Default sender for Mailer::createMail() and mail() mail:reply_to string empty Default Reply-To; an unset message Reply-To falls back to its sender mail:username string empty Shared SMTP login; falls back to From when authentication is enabled mail:password string empty Shared SMTP password or OAuth access token mail:smtp:host string empty Required SMTP hostname or IP mail:smtp:port integer automatic 465 for TLS, 587 for STARTTLS, otherwise 25; mailpit defaults to 1025 mail:smtp:security string auto auto, starttls, tls or none mail:smtp:authentication string auto auto, off, on, login, plain, cram-md5, xoauth2 or oauth mail:smtp:username string inherited Nonempty value overrides the shared username mail:smtp:password string inherited Nonempty value overrides the shared password/token mail:smtp:timeout number 15 Connection timeout in seconds; greater than zero and at most 300 mail:smtp:ca_file string empty Optional readable CA file; system trust is used otherwise

The mailer takes the transport from the container when that class is registered there, and otherwise builds it with make(), so the transport's constructor dependencies are autowired. mail:transport and the shipped DummyTransport require naf/mail 0.2.2 or newer. Sender defaults, text alternatives, SMTP and provider metadata require 0.2.3+. Explicit setFrom() and setReplyTo() calls override the configured defaults.

docs.title: Send through SMTP
docs.text:
The built-in Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\SmtpTransport uses Symfony Mailer. Composer installs that dependency and requires OpenSSL alongside the existing fileinfo and mbstring extensions. Merge this fragment into app/config.php and provide the environment values on the server:

use Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\SmtpTransport;

return [
    'mail' => [
        'transport' => SmtpTransport::class,
        'from' => 'support@example.com',
        'reply_to' => 'support@example.com',
        'username' => 'ENV:MAIL_USERNAME',
        'password' => 'ENV:MAIL_PASSWORD',
        'smtp' => [
            'host' => 'smtp.example.com',
            'port' => 587,
            'security' => 'starttls',
            'authentication' => 'on',
        ],
    ],
];

Authentication requires encryption, a username and a password/token. on negotiates a supported mechanism; select login, plain, cram-md5 or xoauth2 to require one. oauth is an alias for xoauth2; obtaining and refreshing the access token belongs to the application. auto enables authentication when a shared or SMTP-specific login/password is supplied. From alone does not enable it. An empty protocol-specific credential inherits the shared value.

Automatic security selects implicit TLS for port 465, unencrypted delivery for localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1 and mailpit, and STARTTLS for other hosts. TLS certificates and hostnames are always verified. Explicit STARTTLS fails if the server cannot upgrade; use ca_file for a private trusted CA. Unencrypted mode cannot send authentication credentials.

The transport validates configuration and opens a connection only when sending or checking. An incomplete SMTP configuration therefore does not break unrelated pages. To check TLS and login without sending a message, run this fragment after application bootstrap:

use Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\SmtpTransport;

(new SmtpTransport())->checkConnection();

Connection checks may throw configuration or Symfony transport exceptions. Catch Throwable at an administrative boundary and show a suitable message without exposing credentials.

docs.title: Describe provider configuration fields
docs.text:
ConfigurableTransportInterface optionally extends TransportInterface with static configurationFields(): array. A configuration renderer can request metadata without constructing a transport:

use Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\{SmtpTransport, TransportConfiguration};

$fields = TransportConfiguration::fields(SmtpTransport::class);

Each key is a colon-separated configuration path. A description can contain label, type, default, index, options and sensitive. The built-in SMTP metadata supplies choices, port/time limits and a secret flag for its password. Existing transports without the optional interface return an empty description. Mark credentials explicitly as sensitive; metadata does not itself render, validate, persist or redact values.

docs.title: Testing without a mail server
docs.text:
naf/mail ships Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\DummyTransport. It records a copy of every message in memory, returns true and never connects to a mail server. Start from Your first application, install the package and create the directory for the demo script:

composer require naf/mail
mkdir -p bin

docs.title: Select the transport
docs.text:
Select the transport in app/config.php. This is the complete file for the exercise; in an existing application, merge the mail key into your configuration:

app/config.php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

use Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\DummyTransport;

return [
    'mail' => [
        'transport' => DummyTransport::class,
        'from' => 'hello@example.com',
    ],
];

This setting captures every message

With DummyTransport selected, nothing is delivered, in any environment. Choose the transport per environment, for example:

use Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\{DummyTransport, MailTransport};

'mail' => [
    'transport' => getenv('APP_ENV') === 'prod' ? MailTransport::class : DummyTransport::class,
],

docs.title: Read the captured messages
docs.text:
To inspect the messages, the code that sends and the code that checks must use the same DummyTransport instance. Register one shared instance in the container; the mailer then takes it from there. In root bootstrap.php, after requiring vendor/autoload.php and before app()->run(), add:

use Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\DummyTransport;
use function Naf\app;

app()->container()->set(DummyTransport::class, static fn() => new DummyTransport());

The following script sends one message and reads it back. It registers the shared instance itself when the bootstrap does not, so you can run it before changing bootstrap.php:

bin/mail-demo.php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

require dirname(__DIR__) . '/bootstrap.php';

use Naf\Mail\Core\Transport\DummyTransport;
use function Naf\app;
use function Naf\Mail\{mail, mailer};

$container = app()->container();
if (!$container->has(DummyTransport::class)) {
    $container->set(DummyTransport::class, static fn() => new DummyTransport());
}

$message = mail()
    ->addTo('reader@example.com')
    ->setSubject('Hello from NAF')
    ->setContent('<b>A local test message.</b>')
    ->setTextContent('A local test message.');

if (!mailer()->send($message)) {
    throw new RuntimeException('The transport reported a failure.');
}

$messages = $container->get(DummyTransport::class)->getMessages();
echo 'Stored messages: ' . count($messages) . PHP_EOL;
echo 'Subject: ' . $messages[0]->getSubject() . PHP_EOL;
echo 'Sender: ' . $messages[0]->getFrom() . PHP_EOL;
echo 'Text: ' . $messages[0]->getTextContent() . PHP_EOL;

php bin/mail-demo.php

Expected output:

Stored messages: 1
Subject: Hello from NAF
Sender: hello@example.com
Text: A local test message.

getMessages() returns the recorded Mail objects; getRecipients(), getContent(), isHtml() and the other getters show what was submitted. clear() empties the list between test cases. Returning true simulates successful transport acceptance; it does not establish whether real mail would be delivered.

docs.title: Inspect messages after browser requests
docs.text: The in-memory list belongs to the current PHP request/process. A subsequent browser request cannot retrieve the previous request's list. For manual browser testing, use the FileTransport example: it writes a JSON preview to storage/mail/, which remains available after the response or redirect.

docs.title: Real delivery and custom transports
docs.text:
The default MailTransport uses PHP's mail(), which needs a configured delivery system on the server. Use the built-in SMTP transport for direct SMTP. For another provider, implement TransportInterface::sendMail(Mail $mail): bool with your chosen library and select the class in mail:transport:

// app/config.php
'mail' => ['transport' => \App\Mail\SmtpTransport::class],

Constructor dependencies of the transport are autowired. When it needs scalar settings such as a host or password, register a factory under the class name in bootstrap.php; the mailer then uses that registration.

Keep test transports confined to development or tests: their successful return values mean the simulation accepted the message. Constructing a separate new Mailer(...) or calling mailer($transport) returns an independent mailer and does not change the shared mailer().

docs.title: Queued delivery
docs.text:
Delivery can delay the HTTP response. Push the message data to a queue and let a job build and send the message in the worker. Pass plain values such as addresses, a subject and record identifiers rather than the Mail object, and make the job safe to run twice: queue delivery is at least once.

Workers can render mail bodies with naf/view after application boot. Framework 0.2.9+ provides the required guards under CLI; older versions need the registration described in Templates outside HTTP requests.

docs.title: If the result is different
docs.text: What you see What to check mail:transport must name a class implementing … The value is a class name of a class that implements TransportInterface Unable to send mail using PHP mail() PHP's mail() needs a configured delivery program (sendmail_path); use a capture transport locally getMessages() is empty in a test The test reads a different DummyTransport instance; register one shared instance in the container No file appears in storage/mail/ The contact recipe selects FileTransport in mail:transport, and the directory is writable

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
naf/mcp exposes explicitly registered tools over a stateless MCP Streamable HTTP endpoint. Tools are PHP classes with input schemas and handlers. Bearer tokens and tool scopes control access; handlers must still authorize the application data and operations they expose.

This guide requires naf/mcp 0.2.7+, PHP 8.3+ and naf/framework 0.2.8+. Start from a bootstrapped application. The default token store uses a file, not a database. The example below measures files in one application-owned reports directory.

Required packages

In an existing NAF application:

composer require naf/mcp

docs.title: The endpoint
docs.text:
The POST /mcp endpoint implements stateless Streamable HTTP. Clients send Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json, text/event-stream. The default response is JSON. Enable SSE responses in the host's app/config.php return array:

'mcp' => ['transport' => ['streaming' => true]],

Set mcp:transport:streaming back to false to return JSON and invoke ordinary handle() methods. Both modes use the same Streamable HTTP endpoint. The setting controls response streaming, not endpoint installation or authentication. Accepted notifications and client responses receive an empty HTTP 202. Batches and non-object JSON are rejected. Authenticated GET requests receive 405 with Allow: POST: there is no persistent GET event channel, session id, replay or resumability support.

Initialize with a protocolVersion, capabilities object and clientInfo:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"Example client","version":"1.0"}}}

The server negotiates 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26. Send the negotiated MCP-Protocol-Version header on later requests. An unsupported supplied version returns 400. A supplied Origin must match the configured public_url origin or an exact entry in mcp:transport:allowed_origins (list of origin strings, default []); otherwise it returns 403. Without either configuration, supplied Origins are rejected; the caller's Host header does not establish a trusted origin. An absent Origin is accepted for non-browser clients. Bind local development servers to loopback; use a configured public HTTPS origin in production.

StreamingToolInterface extends the ordinary tool contract with stream(array $args): Generator. Keep a working handle() method for JSON mode. Yield Progress values and return the final result:

use Naf\MCP\Support\Progress;
use Naf\MCP\Tools\StreamingToolInterface;

// Add this method to a tool implementing StreamingToolInterface.
public function stream(array $args): \Generator
{
    yield new Progress(0, 1, 'Reading the report');
    $result = $this->handle($args);
    yield new Progress(1, 1, 'Report ready');
    return $result;
}

Progress values must be finite, non-negative and strictly increase. An optional total cannot be smaller than progress. Notifications are sent only when the caller supplies a string or integer params._meta.progressToken. The final JSON-RPC result follows on the same SSE stream. The PSR-7 body reads lazily and the framework emitter sends each message as it becomes available. The plugin sends X-Accel-Buffering: no and Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform. Verify proxy/CDN buffering and compression on the deployed host; PHP's local emitter alone does not prove Internet latency.

MCP 0.2.5 supplies its own narrow csrf_exempt_routes:mcp_server_rpc exemption when naf/form is installed. Keep MCP authentication enabled. A Bearer header alone does not exempt a request from Form's CSRF listener. Older MCP installations with Form 0.2.3+ need that exact route exemption in host configuration; it can be removed after upgrading.

docs.title: A tool
docs.text:
Create the reports directory from the project root:

mkdir -p storage/reports

Create this tool file. Its handler accepts only the reports identifier and rejects unknown arguments. Keep the directory application-owned and perform account-specific access checks when adapting this example to private data.

app/Mcp/GetFolderSize.php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace App\Mcp;

use Naf\MCP\Support\Schema;
use Naf\MCP\Tools\ToolInterface;
use Naf\MCP\Tools\ScopedToolInterface;
use function Naf\log;

final class GetFolderSize implements ToolInterface, ScopedToolInterface
{
    public function name(): string
    {
        return 'get_folder_size';
    }

    public function description(): string
    {
        return 'Returns the size of a folder.';
    }

    public function inputSchema(): array
    {
        return Schema::object()
            ->description($this->description())
            ->additionalProperties(false)
            ->prop('folder', Schema::string()->enum(['reports'])->description('Application folder identifier'))
            ->required('folder')
            ->toArray();
    }

    public function requiredScopes(): array
    {
        return ['folders:read'];
    }

    public function handle(array $args): mixed
    {
        if (($args['folder'] ?? null) !== 'reports' || array_diff(array_keys($args), ['folder']) !== []) {
            throw new \InvalidArgumentException('Expected only folder=reports.');
        }

        $path = BASE_PATH . '/storage/reports';
        if (!is_dir($path)) {
            throw new \RuntimeException('Reports directory is unavailable.');
        }
        $bytes = 0;

        try {
            $it = new \RecursiveIteratorIterator(
                new \RecursiveDirectoryIterator($path, \FilesystemIterator::SKIP_DOTS)
            );

            foreach ($it as $file) {
                if (!$file->isLink() && $file->isFile()) {
                    $bytes += $file->getSize();
                }
            }
        } catch (\RuntimeException $error) {
            log()->error('Reports tool failed: ' . $error->getMessage());
            throw new \RuntimeException('Unable to read reports.');
        }

        return ['folder' => 'reports', 'bytes' => $bytes];
    }
}

Tool and property descriptions are sent to clients. Describe the operation, accepted input and relevant limits so an assistant can select it correctly.

Schema builds the JSON Schema without writing it by hand — object(), string(), integer(), boolean() and array(Schema $items) to start one, then prop(), required(), nullable(), enum(), min(), max(), default(), description() and additionalProperties(). Finish with toArray().

Input schemas are enforced before handlers run. Empty schemas normalize to a closed object; object schemas default to additionalProperties: false. Explicitly allow extra keys when needed. Invalid arguments return JSON-RPC -32602. Keep domain validation and data access checks in handle(); schema validation cannot decide which records a caller may access.

docs.title: Registering it
docs.text:
Register the tool in root bootstrap.php, after autoloading and before app()->run():

use function Naf\MCP\tool;

tool()->register(new App\Mcp\GetFolderSize());

Tools are not discovered by directory scanning. Registration order determines list order; a repeated name() replaces the previous registration. Use unique tool names.

docs.title: What comes back
docs.text:
Returning Naf\MCP\Support\ToolResult::text() or another valid MCP result preserves its content blocks. Associative arrays and objects also populate structuredContent, with a JSON text block for compatibility. Lists remain JSON text. Optional ToolMetadataInterface::metadata() can provide title, annotations, outputSchema and _meta; core name, description and input schema come from the tool contract. A declared output schema is validated against structured content. Handler failures and invalid output are logged and return isError: true with the generic message The tool could not complete the request. Internal exception messages are no longer exposed to callers.

For the folder example, a successful result includes both representations:

{
  "result": {
    "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "{\n    \"folder\": \"reports\",\n    \"bytes\": 14\n}"}],
    "structuredContent": {"folder": "reports", "bytes": 14},
    "isError": false
  }
}

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
The default mcp:auth:driver is file. The endpoint wants a Bearer token:

Authorization: Bearer mcp_...

Tokens live in storage/mcp/tokens.json — set MCP_TOKEN_FILE in the environment, or mcp:auth:token_file in the configuration, to keep them somewhere else. Only a hash is stored, so a stolen file is not a set of working tokens.

With naf/cli installed the plugin registers three commands:

vendor/bin/naf mcp:token:create "Local AI client" --scope "folders:read"
vendor/bin/naf mcp:token:list
vendor/bin/naf mcp:token:revoke tok_...

Note the two prefixes. The secret a client sends starts with mcp_ and is shown once, at creation; the id you revoke by starts with tok_ and is what list prints. Losing the secret requires issuing a replacement token.

From application code:

use function Naf\MCP\tokens;

$created = tokens()->create('Local AI client', ['folders:read']);

echo $created->plainToken;      // mcp_… — shown once, only the hash is kept
echo $created->record->id;      // tok_… — what you revoke by

For an isolated local endpoint, authentication can be disabled in app/config.php:

return ['mcp' => ['auth' => ['enabled' => false]]];

This allows every caller that can reach the endpoint to invoke every registered tool, including scoped tools. Keep authentication enabled for publicly reachable endpoints.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
A token carries scopes; a tool can demand them by implementing ScopedToolInterface alongside ToolInterface:

use Naf\MCP\Tools\ScopedToolInterface;

final class ArticleSearchTool implements ToolInterface, ScopedToolInterface
{
    public function requiredScopes(): array
    {
        return ['articles:read'];
    }

    // …the four ToolInterface methods
}

With the default File-Token driver, three patterns are understood: * for everything, an exact scope like articles:read, and a prefix wildcard like articles:*. A scoped tool requires at least one of its declared scopes. If a token matches none, the tool is omitted from tools/list and direct calls return HTTP 403. Enforce stricter combinations inside the handler when an operation requires several grants.

docs.title: What a client sees
docs.text:
Initialize using the request above, then send notifications/initialized without an id. The notification receives HTTP 202. The initialize response announces tools capability and the negotiated protocol version; tool definitions follow in tools/list. Send MCP-Protocol-Version with that version on subsequent requests and keep both Accept media types.

Request the tools themselves to receive the definitions this token may see:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list" }

{
  "result": {
    "tools": [
      {
        "name": "get_folder_size",
        "description": "Returns the size of a folder.",
        "inputSchema": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": { "folder": { "type": "string", "enum": ["reports"] } },
          "required": ["folder"],
          "additionalProperties": false
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

And calls one:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "get_folder_size",
    "arguments": { "folder": "reports" }
  }
}

docs.title: OAuth authentication and personal tools
docs.text:
Install or update the OAuth integration together with MCP:

composer require naf/mcp:^0.2.7 naf/oauth-server:^0.2.6 --with-all-dependencies

OAuth remains optional when using the default File-Token driver. MCP 0.2.7 excludes OAuth Server versions before 0.2.6 through Composer conflict metadata. Configure the OAuth database, scopes, public URL and canonical audience. Set these fragments in the host configuration, replacing the example URLs:

'public_url' => 'https://tools.example.com',
'oauth_server' => [
    'name' => 'Example tools',
    'audience' => 'https://tools.example.com/mcp',
    'scopes' => ['account:read' => ['label' => 'Read your account', 'permission' => 'account.read']],
],
'mcp' => [
    'auth' => ['enabled' => true, 'driver' => 'oauth'],
    'oauth' => [
        'resource' => 'https://tools.example.com/mcp',
        'authorization_servers' => ['https://tools.example.com'],
        'scopes_supported' => ['account:read'],
    ],
],

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as MCP client
    participant P as Resource metadata
    participant O as OAuth server
    participant M as POST /mcp
    C->>P: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
    P-->>C: resource and authorization server
    C->>O: authorization code with PKCE and resource
    O-->>C: access token for that resource
    C->>M: tools/call with Bearer token
    M->>M: token, audience, scopes, permissions
    M-->>C: tool result, or 401 / 403

mcp:auth:driver defaults to file; oauth delegates bearer validation to the existing OAuth ResourceServer. Expired, revoked, wrong-audience and deleted-account tokens fail. Current user permissions filter the token's usable scopes. A browser session never supplies a missing bearer identity. PRM is public at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp; absent resource/server configuration returns 404. Use naf/oauth-server 0.2.6+ for OAuth authentication. It includes the conventional authorization-server metadata and resource-bound code exchange needed by Alexa, together with strict scope-policy and PKCE validation.

docs.title: Request lifetime
docs.text:
MCP 0.2.7 passes the authenticator's supplied PSR-7 request directly to the OAuth resource server, including ordinary RequestInterface instances. A shared authenticator evaluates each request's Authorization header: a missing, invalid or different token cannot inherit the preceding caller's identity or scopes.

For a custom adapter, pass the PSR-7 request being authorized to the configured Naf\MCP\Auth\AuthenticatorInterface. This fragment assumes $authenticator is that injected service and $request is the supplied request:

$identity = $authenticator->authenticate($request);

The OAuth driver returns a Naf\MCP\Auth\McpIdentity for a usable token and null when it cannot authenticate it. Acquire this identity for each request. Follow the OAuth server's request-lifetime rules when sharing services in a custom adapter; other request-bound dependencies also need an appropriate lifetime.

docs.title: Personal tools and discovery
docs.text:
Personal tools implement UserToolInterface in addition to the ordinary tool/scoped contracts. Calling one without a linked user returns HTTP 401; a linked user missing the required scopes receives 403. Neither response includes WWW-Authenticate, matching the Alexa requirement. Get the authenticated user through Naf\OAuth\Server\token()->user(), not auth()'s browser session. OAuth scope names are matched literally: * and notes:* do not grant any other scope. The File-Token driver's documented wildcards remain available. A tool's scope list keeps its any-of semantics for both drivers; marking a tool with UserToolInterface is an additional linked-user requirement, not another scope alternative.

The optional mcp:auth:discovery_scope (default null) lets an unlinked service identity with that scope see tool definitions, including personal tools. It does not grant execution. Use separate service and account-linking clients and never give a service registration user scopes. Alexa+ supplies this profile and its setup checks.

docs.title: Grouping behaviours in one tool
docs.text:
A tool may take an action argument and branch on it:

->prop('action', Schema::string()->enum(['analyze', 'summary', 'details']))

This keeps related operations together instead of spreading five near-identical tools across the list a model has to choose from. Use enum() when you do it: the alternatives then travel in the schema, and the model picks from them rather than guessing a verb.

docs.title: Files a tool needs
docs.text:
FilesystemStore provides local file operations relative to an application-owned root. It rejects textual .. traversal and unsupported path characters, and caps each write at 5,000,000 bytes by default:

use Naf\MCP\Support\FilesystemStore;

$store = new FilesystemStore(BASE_PATH . '/storage/mcp/tools', maxBytes: 1_000_000);

$store->write('folder-size/cache.json', $json);
$entry = $store->read('folder-size/cache.json');

Construct it explicitly; there is no default root or container binding. Methods return arrays:

Method Result and failures read() Path, encoding, content and bytes; throws if the file is missing or unreadable write() Success, path and bytes; throws on an oversized write or write failure list() Entries with path/type and file sizes; throws for a non-directory delete() Success, path and whether a file was deleted; a missing file is not an error

Invalid paths and unsupported encodings throw. The default cap limits each write's bytes, not total directory size or the resulting size of an appended file.

The store is not itself an MCP tool. Keep its root and parent directories under application control, without caller-created symlinks. Its path checks are not a filesystem isolation boundary for hostile local writers. Your tool must authorize operations and validate paths.

docs.title: Request sizes and execution limits
docs.text:
MCP 0.2.6+ limits the JSON request body to 1 MiB before decoding. Set mcp:transport:max_request_bytes to a positive integer in bytes below PHP_INT_MAX:

// In the array returned by app/config.php:
'mcp' => ['transport' => ['max_request_bytes' => 262144]],

A request exceeding the limit receives HTTP 413. The limit also applies without Content-Length, and the controller reads at most the limit plus one byte before deciding. It bounds the controller's input buffer; decoded objects, schemas and tool results consume additional memory. Configure request limits at the proxy and PHP layer too, before PHP accepts and parses input.

Streaming does not impose an application execution deadline. Bound work in the tool's service, set PHP worker timeouts, and limit concurrent requests at the proxy. Verify progress flushing and disconnect behavior through that deployed proxy. See the Alexa deployment checks for the authentication and streaming boundary.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
This plugin implements tools, not MCP resources. It does not register resources/list, resources/read or resources/write. Add explicit tools for supported application operations.

The MCP Streamable HTTP specification describes the client transport contract.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
naf/monitoring records declared counters, gauges and histograms, exports them to StatsD or DogStatsD, and can decorate a PSR-3 logger. The application chooses its metrics, labels and collector. The default exporter performs no network I/O.

Use this guide in an existing NAF application, with PHP 8.3+ and Framework 0.2.3 or newer.

NAF discovers the installed Composer plugin automatically. Application code uses Naf\Monitoring\monitor() or injects Naf\Monitoring\Monitor. Both share the same service. No application route, daemon or scheduler is installed by the plugin.

Required packages

In an existing NAF application:

composer require naf/monitoring

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Use a disposable NAF application for this example. Replace app/config.php with the following file; when adding monitoring to an existing application, merge the monitoring entry into its current configuration.

app/config.php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

return [
    'monitoring' => [
        'metrics' => [
            'orders.created' => ['type' => 'counter', 'labels' => ['channel']],
        ],
    ],
];

Create bin/monitoring-demo.php:

bin/monitoring-demo.php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

use Naf\Monitoring\Exporters\InMemoryExporter;
use Naf\Monitoring\MetricExporterInterface;

use function Naf\app;
use function Naf\Monitoring\monitor;

define('BASE_PATH', dirname(__DIR__));
require BASE_PATH . '/vendor/autoload.php';

$application = app();
$exporter = new InMemoryExporter();
$application->container()->set(MetricExporterInterface::class, $exporter);

monitor('orders.created', ['channel' => 'web'])->increment(3);
monitor()->flush();

foreach ($exporter->drain() as $measurement) {
    echo $measurement->definition->name, ': ', $measurement->value,
        ' (channel=', $measurement->labels['channel'], ')', PHP_EOL;
}

Run the example from the application root:

php bin/monitoring-demo.php

Expected output:

orders.created: 3 (channel=web)

Register the exporter override before the first metric call. The helper and an injected Monitor share that service. The in-memory exporter lets you inspect measurements without a collector; configure StatsD or DogStatsD for production collection.

docs.title: Declare your metrics
docs.text:
Merge these entries into the array returned by app/config.php:

<?php
use Naf\Monitoring\Exporters\StatsDExporter;

return ['monitoring' => [
    'exporter' => StatsDExporter::class,
    'exporter_options' => [
        'host' => '127.0.0.1',
        'port' => 8125,
        'prefix' => 'shop',
        'protocol' => 'statsd',
        'maxDatagramBytes' => 512,
        'timeout' => 0.05,
    ],
    'labels' => ['service' => 'shop', 'environment' => 'prod'],
    'batch_size' => 256,
    'metrics' => [
        'orders.created' => ['type' => 'counter', 'labels' => ['channel']],
        'queue.depth' => ['type' => 'gauge'],
        'checkout.duration' => ['type' => 'histogram', 'unit' => 's'],
    ],
    'http' => true,
    'logging' => [
        'enabled' => true,
        'min_level' => 'warning',
        'count' => true,
    ],
]];

The default exporter is Naf\Monitoring\Exporters\NullExporter, with no network I/O. Default labels and custom metrics are empty; HTTP and logging are disabled. Changing the configured exporter keeps the metric calls in your application intact.

Type Method Meaning counter increment(int\|float $amount = 1): void Add a nonnegative delta; never a cumulative total gauge set(int\|float $value): void Set the current value, including negative values histogram observe(int\|float $value): void Record a nonnegative sample in the declared unit Time histogram measure(callable $operation): mixed Run and time a callback; return its result

measure() requires unit s or ms, uses a monotonic clock, records failed operations too and preserves their exception. observe() accepts an already measured value in the declared unit. Values must be finite; NaN and infinity fail. An undeclared metric or a method incompatible with its type throws immediately.

use function Naf\Monitoring\monitor;

monitor('orders.created')->increment();
monitor('orders.created', ['channel' => 'web'])->increment(5);
monitor('queue.depth')->set(42);
monitor('checkout.duration')->observe(0.125); // seconds

$result = monitor('checkout.duration')->measure(fn() => $checkout->run());

The metric definitions belong to the application configuration, not to request input. Names contain 1–120 ASCII letters, digits, _ and ., start with a letter, and cannot contain the reserved __labels segment. Units contain up to 24 ASCII letters, digits, _ or /. Built-in metric names below cannot be redeclared.

docs.title: Labels and request isolation
docs.text:
Per-metric labels declare the allowed keys, not their values. Omitted labels remain absent. Global monitoring:labels apply to every metric and exported log; global keys cannot overlap any declared per-metric keys, including built-in keys.

Each helper call owns its label values. Reusing a returned metric retains its own labels; subsequent calls do not change it. There is no mutable global request context to leak into another queue job.

Label names start with a letter and contain at most 32 letters, digits or _. Values are strings, integers or booleans; normalized values contain 1–80 ASCII letters, digits, _, ., / or -. Booleans become true and false. There may be at most 16 global and metric labels combined. Protocol delimiters and control characters are rejected rather than silently changing a metric's identity.

Use bounded values such as channel, route name and status. Unique user IDs, order IDs and full request URLs create a new time series per value. The character and length limits do not limit the number of distinct series in your backend.

docs.title: StatsD and DogStatsD
docs.text:
The shipped StatsDExporter uses UDP to a numeric IPv4/IPv6 address. The default is 127.0.0.1:8125. Hostnames are rejected so DNS lookup cannot stall a request; resolve the agent address in deployment configuration or inject a custom DatagramTransportInterface. The socket opens lazily at export and uses non-blocking writes. The connection timeout is in seconds, greater than zero and at most one second.

Behavior statsd dogstatsd Counter c, delta c, delta Gauge g, absolute value g, absolute value Histogram ms, requires s or ms; seconds convert to milliseconds h, retains the declared unit/value Labels Sorted, hex-encoded suffix in the metric name Sorted native \|#key:value tags Aggregation/buckets Configured in the StatsD agent Configured in the DogStatsD agent/backend

For example, orders.created with channel=web is sent as orders.created.__labels.6368616e6e656c.776562:1|c in plain StatsD, or orders.created:1|c|#channel:web in DogStatsD, before any configured prefix. The reserved suffix and hex encoding preserve distinct label values and keys. Classic StatsD cannot carry native tags, unit metadata or arbitrary histograms; declaring a non-time histogram with that exporter fails during service creation. Configure display units in the backend for DogStatsD histograms.

Plain StatsD treats signed gauges as deltas. Negative absolute gauges therefore send a reset to zero followed by the negative value in the same datagram. Packets contain whole records, never fragments of a measurement or its reset pair. maxDatagramBytes defaults to 512 and accepts 64–65507; choose a limit appropriate for your network MTU. A single oversize measurement fails the batch and is diagnosed.

Protocol references: StatsD metric types and DogStatsD datagrams.

docs.title: PSR-3 logging
docs.text:
Enable monitoring:logging:enabled to wrap the logger currently registered under Psr\Log\LoggerInterface. Continue using the normal helper:

use function Naf\log;

log()->info('Order accepted');
log()->warning('Inventory below threshold', ['remaining' => 3]);
log()->error('Checkout failed', ['exception' => $exception]);

Every call still reaches the original logger. The monitoring copy is filtered by min_level, which defaults to warning and accepts all eight PSR-3 levels: debug, info, notice, warning, error, critical, alert, emergency. It includes the chosen severity and all higher severities. Invalid levels fail.

With count: true, each qualifying log increments logs.total with its level. Log messages, exception texts and context values never become metric labels. StatsD transports metrics only: enabling the logger does not send raw log messages to a StatsD agent.

For structured log delivery, optionally register a LogExporterInterface service before the first use of the monitor, or configure log_exporter as its class name and log_exporter_options as named constructor arguments. Its export(array $records) receives LogRecord objects with the original message, PSR-3 context, severity, global labels and a Unix timestamp in seconds. The metric and log destinations are attempted independently. Set logging:count to false for log export alone.

Records retain PHP context objects by reference until the batch is exported. Avoid mutating them before flushing; a custom exporter owns serialization, exception formatting, field selection and redaction. There is no bundled HTTP/OTLP log exporter in this first version. Export failures and diagnostics are guarded against recursive monitoring; the default diagnostic path uses PHP error_log() directly.

If your host replaces the logger after plugin boot, wrap that final logger explicitly before constructing its consumers. Keep automatic decoration disabled in that case:

use Naf\Monitoring\{Monitor, MonitoringLogger};
use Psr\Log\LoggerInterface;
use function Naf\app;

$container = app()->container();
$original = $container->get(LoggerInterface::class); // After your custom registration.
$container->set(LoggerInterface::class, static fn() => new MonitoringLogger(
    $original,
    $container->get(Monitor::class),
    minLevel: 'error',
));

Register overrides before resolving Monitor or the decorated logger. A later rebinding cannot replace a dependency already held by an instantiated service.

docs.title: HTTP instrumentation
docs.text:
With monitoring:http enabled, the plugin listens to the existing NAF request, route, exception and response events. It records:

Metric Type/unit Labels http.requests Counter method, route, status http.duration Histogram, seconds method, route, status http.exceptions Counter None logs.total Counter; requires logging/count enabled level

Duration begins at REQUEST_START and normally ends at RESPONSE_END, after the response body is written. It excludes bootstrap and the final monitoring flush. Threshold-triggered exports during the request remain part of its processing time. It measures server processing, not the client's download time. A shutdown fallback handles skipped/interrupted response-end listeners without counting a request twice; when a response was observed, it uses PHP's emitted status for that fallback.

Routes use their registered name, never the concrete URL. Unmatched routes use unmatched, unnamed routes use unnamed, and names outside the portable label syntax use other. Unrecognized HTTP methods use OTHER. Exception counting is once per observed request and includes exceptions raised for normal HTTP errors such as a missing route. It covers the NAF exception event and observed fatal shutdowns; it is not a global record of every caught or uncaught PHP exception.

docs.title: Buffering, workers and failures
docs.text:
The shared metric/log buffer flushes when it reaches batch_size records, at normal response end and at PHP shutdown. The default is 256, with an allowed range of 1–10000. The bound is a record count, not a byte limit on arbitrary structured log contexts. Custom exporters must also bound their own work and memory.

Long-running workers explicitly flush in the job's existing lifecycle:

use function Naf\Monitoring\monitor;

try {
    $job->handle();
} finally {
    monitor()->flush();
}

This is an application fragment, not a new NAF worker API. There is no periodic background flush or queue dependency. Retained metric objects keep their labels, so create job-specific metrics inside each job. The InMemoryExporter used in tests also needs draining between jobs if retained indefinitely.

Export happens synchronously at flush points. UDP is best-effort: a successful socket write does not confirm delivery or collector health. Batches are removed before export and never retried, preventing repeated counter increments. A partial network failure can deliver some datagrams and lose others. Process termination, early bootstrap errors, memory exhaustion and a prior shutdown handler that exits can prevent the final flush. This is telemetry, not an audit trail or billing ledger.

Runtime export exceptions are caught and increase monitor()->failedBatches(). The plugin's default diagnostic callback writes to PHP's error_log(). Override monitoring:on_error with a callback receiving (Throwable $error, string $signal); $signal is metrics or logs. Keep that callback independent of this monitor. API/configuration mistakes still throw early. measure() preserves an application's return value or exception even if exporting the timing fails.

docs.title: Custom exporters and multiple destinations
docs.text:
Implement MetricExporterInterface with two methods:

  • validate(MetricDefinition $definition): void rejects unsupported types/units when the monitoring service is constructed, including built-in definitions.
  • export(array $measurements): void receives a batch of Measurement objects. Each contains its definition, numeric value and normalized labels. It sends once and throws on failure. Counters represent deltas, gauges absolute values and histograms individual observations.

Use exporter and exporter_options for a class constructed through NAF's normal autowiring, or bind MetricExporterInterface explicitly in root bootstrap.php, before app()->run() and before the monitor is resolved. For example:

use Naf\Monitoring\MetricExporterInterface;
use Naf\Monitoring\Exporters\{CompositeExporter, InMemoryExporter, StatsDExporter};
use function Naf\app;

$capture = new InMemoryExporter();
app()->container()->set(MetricExporterInterface::class, new CompositeExporter([
    new StatsDExporter(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 8125),
    $capture,
]));

CompositeExporter attempts every destination even when one fails. A failed composite batch increments failedBatches() once; successful destinations are not retried. All destinations must support the declared metrics.

For an HTTP adapter, inject a PSR-18 client, such as naf/client, and keep URL, authentication and format inside that adapter. Bind Psr\Http\Client\ClientInterface to the configured client in the host; the monitoring plugin does not install an HTTP stack. An OTLP adapter should use the existing OpenTelemetry SDK. A future Prometheus pull adapter additionally needs aggregation across PHP requests and processes; no /metrics endpoint is shipped here.

docs.title: Testing without a collector
docs.text:
use Naf\Monitoring\{MetricDefinition, MetricType, Monitor};
use Naf\Monitoring\Exporters\InMemoryExporter;

$exporter = new InMemoryExporter();
$monitor = new Monitor($exporter, [
    new MetricDefinition('orders.created', MetricType::Counter),
]);
$monitor->metric('orders.created')->increment(3);
$monitor->flush();

$measurements = $exporter->drain();
assert($measurements[0]->value === 3);

measurements() inspects retained records; drain() returns and clears them. The in-memory exporter defaults to a capacity of 10000 records and throws when full. Through Monitor, that failure is counted and the failed batch is dropped. NullExporter discards exported batches and performs no I/O.

The package suite tests these APIs, the PSR-3 severity matrix, independent export failures, protocol bytes, bounds and label isolation. Real loopback UDP and HTTP/CLI tests verify Composer discovery, host overrides, response behavior and flushing against the published framework. See AGENTS.md for the development commands.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Add these keys below monitoring in app/config.php. Configuration merges with the plugin defaults before the monitoring service is resolved.

Key Type Default Effect monitoring:exporter class string Naf\Monitoring\Exporters\NullExporter Metric exporter implementing MetricExporterInterface monitoring:exporter_options array [] Named constructor arguments for the selected metric exporter monitoring:log_exporter class string or null null Optional structured log exporter implementing LogExporterInterface monitoring:log_exporter_options array [] Named constructor arguments for the log exporter monitoring:labels array [] Constant service/environment labels on metrics and exported logs monitoring:batch_size integer 256 Shared record-count flush threshold, from 1 to 10000 monitoring:metrics array [] Metric names mapped to type, optional unit and allowed labels monitoring:http boolean false Enables request, duration and exception metrics through NAF events monitoring:on_error callable or null null Independent callback receiving the export exception and metrics or logs; null uses PHP error_log() monitoring:logging:enabled boolean false Decorates the currently registered PSR-3 logger monitoring:logging:min_level string warning Lowest severity copied into monitoring monitoring:logging:count boolean true Adds logs.total for qualifying logs when decoration is enabled

When selecting StatsDExporter, its monitoring:exporter_options keys are:

Key Type Default Effect host string 127.0.0.1 Numeric IPv4/IPv6 collector address port integer 8125 UDP destination port, from 1 to 65535 prefix string empty Prefix using the metric-name syntax protocol string statsd statsd or dogstatsd wire format maxDatagramBytes integer 512 Whole-record datagram limit, from 64 to 65507 bytes timeout number 0.05 Socket connection timeout in seconds, greater than zero and at most one transport DatagramTransportInterface or null null Explicit transport override; null constructs UdpTransport

InMemoryExporter accepts a positive capacity constructor option, defaulting to 10000 retained measurements. Drain it between tests or worker jobs.

docs.title: API details
docs.text:
Import the helper from Naf\Monitoring:

use function Naf\Monitoring\monitor;

// monitor(?string $name = null, array $labels = []): Monitor|Metric
$service = monitor();
$metric = monitor('orders.created', ['channel' => 'web']);

Calling monitor() returns the shared Monitor; supplying a name creates a Metric with its own normalized label values. Labels without a name throw InvalidArgumentException. Monitor::metric(string $name, array $labels = []): Metric provides the same lookup on an injected service. Metric mutation methods and timing requirements are listed under Declare your metrics.

Monitor::flush(): void exports pending records once. Monitor::failedBatches(): int returns the number of failed metric or log batches. The extension contracts use these namespaces:

Contract Namespace Metric batches Naf\Monitoring\MetricExporterInterface Structured log batches Naf\Monitoring\LogExporterInterface Datagram transport Naf\Monitoring\Transport\DatagramTransportInterface

See the generated function index and configuration reference.

docs.title: If the result is different
docs.text: Symptom Check No metric reaches the collector The default exporter is NullExporter. Select a real exporter, check its numeric address/port and call flush() in long-running jobs. A successful UDP write does not confirm delivery. An undeclared metric or label throws Add the metric and allowed label keys to application configuration before the monitor is resolved. A histogram is rejected by StatsD Plain StatsD accepts only time histograms in s or ms. Use DogStatsD for other histogram units. HTTP or log metrics are absent Enable monitoring:http or monitoring:logging:enabled and inspect the log severity threshold. A custom exporter binding is ignored Register it before the first use of Monitor or the decorated logger. Existing objects retain their dependencies. Export failures recur Inspect failedBatches() and the independent diagnostic callback; bound the exporter work and record sizes. Failed batches are discarded.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Application lifecycle for bootstrap timing and service registration.
  • Dependency injection for factories and overrides.
  • Events for request and response hooks.
  • Queues and workers for background job lifetimes.
  • HTTP client for PSR-18 adapters.

docs.title: OAuth client
docs.text:
naf/oauth-client integrates external OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect sign-in with NAF Auth. It supplies protocol routes and verification; the application configures providers and maps external identities to local accounts.

Before enabling a provider, configure the public URL, credentials, local account source and link storage. Run the setup and migration steps below, then verify the complete redirect and callback flow. Provider API access after login is a separate opt-in integration.

Required packages

In an existing NAF application:

composer require naf/oauth-client

Also installs these transitive dependencies: naf/auth, naf/session.

docs.title: Protocol verification
docs.text:
ExternalIdentity contains the verified issuer, subject and claims. Map that external identity to a local account before completing sign-in.

The plugin applies these protocol checks:

Check Behavior PKCE S256, always, for confidential clients too state random, stored server-side, consumed once nonce issued and checked against the ID token Signature always verified against the provider's published keys, wherever there is an ID token Algorithm pinned to what the provider publishes, never read from the token's own header Claims iss, aud, exp, iat, nonce, sub are checked; azp is checked when present Metadata the document has to name the issuer you configured before anything in it is used Redirect URI derived from your public URL, sent exactly, never taken from a request Transport https only, and no redirects followed while credentials are in flight Key rotation an unknown key id reloads the key set, once, with a cooldown

A provider whose keys cannot be read makes the login fail. It never makes the check optional.

The configured issuer establishes which provider is trusted. Discovery metadata must name that issuer before its endpoints and keys are used. Unavailable keys do not disable token verification; they cause the login to fail.

Provider tokens are not stored by default. Enable encrypted token storage only when the application needs to call provider APIs after login; see Calling the provider afterwards.

docs.title: Google
docs.text:
Add these keys to the array returned by app/config.php:

// app/config.php
return [
    'public_url' => 'https://example.com',
    'auth' => [
        'users'  => ['model' => App\Models\User::class],
        'logins' => [
            'google' => [
                'client_id'     => $_ENV['GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID'],
                'client_secret' => $_ENV['GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET'],
            ],
        ],
    ],
];

The configuration selects the local account model, public URL and external login. The plugin registers callback routes and uses the configured account and session services. Create the link table using the migration steps in this chapter.

The diagnostic commands need composer require naf/cli. For the API-call example later, also install naf/client.

Inspect the callback URL to register in the provider console:

vendor/bin/naf oauth:discover google

It reads the provider's metadata, proves the setup resolves, and prints the callback URL to paste into their console.

public_url is required and has no default. Inside a request the only candidates are the Host and X-Forwarded-* headers, and those are set by whoever is calling. Every redirect URI is built from this one value, so it is stated once rather than guessed.

docs.title: One provider, several logins
docs.text:
The key names the login; driver says which provider is behind it. Keeping them apart is what lets you offer the same provider twice under names of your choosing:

'logins' => [
    'staff'    => ['driver' => 'microsoft', 'tenant' => 'acme.example', 'client_id' => …, 'client_secret' => …],
    'partners' => ['driver' => 'microsoft', 'tenant' => 'partner.example', 'client_id' => …, 'client_secret' => …],
],

Each gets its own callback (/auth/staff/callback, /auth/partners/callback), its own button and its own credentials. Without a driver, the key is the driver — which is why google above needs nothing else.

docs.title: Microsoft
docs.text:
Microsoft needs one more thing: which accounts may sign in.

'microsoft' => [
    'client_id'     => $_ENV['MS_CLIENT_ID'],
    'client_secret' => $_ENV['MS_CLIENT_SECRET'],
    'tenant'        => '8f3a1c94-…',   // directory id, or a verified domain
],

A single named tenant pins the issuer by itself. The multi-tenant values — common, organizations, consumers — mean any organisation in the world may sign in, so they will not start without you saying who:

'tenant'          => 'common',
'allowed_tenants' => ['8f3a1c94-…', 'b21d…'],   // or ['*'] to accept everyone

Without allowed_tenants the setup raises a ConfigurationException naming the key. This is deliberate: with common, Microsoft's discovery document gives its issuer as a template, and the real issuer is only known from the token's own tenant id. Substituting it is safe because the tenant is then checked against your list.

docs.title: Any other OpenID Connect provider
docs.text:
Configure the issuer. Endpoints and signing keys are obtained from its discovery document.

'keycloak' => [
    'issuer'        => 'https://id.example.com/realms/main',
    'client_id'     => …,
    'client_secret' => …,
],

docs.title: GitHub, and other providers without OpenID Connect
docs.text:
'github' => [
    'client_id'     => $_ENV['GITHUB_CLIENT_ID'],
    'client_secret' => $_ENV['GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET'],
],

GitHub has no discovery document and issues no ID token, so its endpoints are named in the preset rather than read from it. Its quirks are handled for you: the credentials go where GitHub documents them, its API version header is sent, and an address the person has not made public is fetched from their verified address list instead of coming back empty.

Naming a profile endpoint does not make a provider plain OAuth2. Protocol and profile are separate: give an OpenID Connect provider a userinfo_url and it stays OpenID Connect — the ID token is verified first, the profile is fetched afterwards, and it is only accepted if it describes the same subject. It adds to a verified identity; it never establishes one.

A provider is plain OAuth2 when it has no issuer. Such a provider takes three URLs and, if it does not call its identifier sub, the field that holds it:

'acme' => [
    'client_id'     => …,
    'client_secret' => …,
    'authorize_url' => 'https://acme.test/oauth/authorize',
    'token_url'     => 'https://acme.test/oauth/token',
    'userinfo_url'  => 'https://acme.test/api/me',
    'subject_field' => 'user_id',
],

For GitLab, select the OpenID Connect path with issuer set to https://gitlab.com, together with the client credentials and application settings described above.

docs.title: Two trust paths, and the difference between them
docs.text:
With OpenID Connect the provider signs a statement addressed to this application, and both the signature and the address are verified. Without it there is nothing to sign: the identity comes from an authenticated call to the provider's API with the access token just exchanged for the code.

Plain OAuth 2.0 sign-in relies on the authorization-code exchange and an authenticated profile request. It has no signed ID token with an audience and nonce to verify. Use OpenID Connect where the provider supports it.

Plain OAuth 2.0 identities use oauth:<provider key> as their issuer key. Renaming that configuration key detaches existing account links. OpenID Connect links use the verified issuer.

docs.title: When a provider rotates your client secret
docs.text:
Update the configured client secret and deploy it before the provider retires the old one. Client IDs, callback URLs and account links remain associated with the same provider.

The secret is read from configuration when needed. Metadata and key caches do not store it.

Coordinate the change with the provider's rotation procedure. When the provider is a NAF OAuth server, its overlap window allows the client deployment to switch credentials:

vendor/bin/naf oauth:client:rotate-secret <client-id>

Deploy the new secret within the overlap window. A server-side --now rotation invalidates the old secret immediately; clients using it fail until their configuration is updated.

docs.title: Validate provider setup
docs.text:
vendor/bin/naf oauth:doctor

It verifies the dependencies, the public URL, the user model and its contract, the link table, and every configured login — including whether the provider's metadata is reachable and belongs to the issuer you configured. It prints the callback URL to register, and never prints a secret.

docs.title: Explicit client configuration
docs.text: oauth:providers is the previous spelling of auth:logins and still works; it is used when auth:logins is absent, and the error messages then name the keys you actually wrote. auth:providers likewise still names account sources explicitly. Nothing has to be migrated.

docs.title: Configuration defaults
docs.text: callback_url, scope, label, after_login, error_route, the table name and the cache location are derived or defaulted. Set them when you actually need something else.

docs.title: Render a sign-in button
docs.text:
use function Naf\OAuth\Client\oauth_button;

<?= oauth_button('google') ?>                          <!-- "Mit Google anmelden" -->
<?= oauth_button('google', 'Continue with Google') ?>  <!-- explicit text wins -->
<?= oauth_button('google', next: '/projects/7') ?>     <!-- land there afterwards -->

The wording is settled highest-first: what you pass in, then your own oauth/button.phtml in the application's view directory, then oauth:providers:<key>:label, then the provider's own name. Copy the shipped view to change the markup — yours wins, and nothing in the central configuration has to change for it.

The button label affects display only; it does not change protocol identifiers or callback URLs.

docs.title: Registered routes
docs.text:
Shipped, named, and off with 'oauth' => ['routes' => false]:

Route Purpose GET /auth/{provider} start a login GET /auth/{provider}/callback what the provider sends back GET /auth/{provider}/connect attach this provider to the account already signed in

All three take ?next=/somewhere — always a local path. Anything else falls back to oauth:after_login, and "anything else" includes embedded control characters: browsers strip tabs and newlines while normalising a URL, so /\r//evil.test would otherwise arrive as //evil.test.

A provider reporting a failure is treated like any other answer: its state is checked and consumed. A cancelled login therefore ends rather than sitting pending until it expires, and nobody can drive the callback by appending ?error= to it.

A refused login redirects to oauth:error_route with the reason flashed into the session as oauth_error, rather than raising an error page. A cancelled login is something a person did, not a server fault:

<?php if ($reason = session()->getFlash('oauth_error')): ?>
    <p><?= $reason === 'not_linked'
        ? 'No account is linked to that login yet.'
        : 'That login could not be completed.' ?></p>
<?php endif ?>

docs.title: Form CSRF tokens after external login
docs.text:
When the host also uses naf/form, rotate its CSRF token after external authentication, as with password login. Auth 0.2.3 rotates session state but does not rotate Form's token; OAuth Client 0.2.4's shipped callback does not perform that host integration either. Otherwise a token rendered before sign-in remains valid afterwards.

With Form 0.2.3+, call csrf()->generate() after a successful application-owned callback. For the shipped account mapping and callback behavior, a thin host route can delegate to OAuthController and perform that rotation. Set 'oauth' => ['routes' => false] in the application configuration, then register all three named routes in app/routes.php:

use Naf\OAuth\Client\Controllers\OAuthController;
use Psr\Http\Message\ResponseInterface;
use function Naf\app;
use function Naf\Auth\auth;
use function Naf\Form\csrf;
use function Naf\route;

route()->add('GET', '/auth/{provider}', [OAuthController::class, 'start'], 'oauth.start');
route()->add('GET', '/auth/{provider}/connect', [OAuthController::class, 'connect'], 'oauth.connect');
route()->add('GET', '/auth/{provider}/callback', static function (string $provider): ResponseInterface {
    $response = app()->container()->make(OAuthController::class)->callback($provider);
    if (auth()->check()) {
        csrf()->generate();
    }

    return $response;
}, 'oauth.callback');

Protocol verification and account linking remain in the plugin. A refused callback does not authenticate a guest; an already signed-in member also receives a fresh token after the handler. Forms and other tabs holding the old token must reload before their next write. Check the complete login flow: a pre-login token must fail afterwards, while a freshly rendered form succeeds.

docs.title: Map an external identity to an account
docs.text:
External login maps an issuer/subject pair to an application account:

  • An existing link loads and signs in the linked account.
  • With auto-registration enabled, the configured callback creates an account and the plugin links it before signing in.
  • Otherwise, login fails with not_linked. The user can sign in locally and connect the provider.

To enable auto-registration, configure the account creation callback:

'oauth' => ['accounts' => [
    'auto_register' => true,
    'create' => static fn(ExternalIdentity $external) => $users->create([
        'email' => $external->email,
        'name'  => $external->name,
    ]),
]],

With several account sources registered in auth:providers, name the one that owns external logins in oauth:accounts:provider. With one, it is used without being named.

docs.title: Identity-link integrity
docs.text:
Identities are keyed on (issuer, subject), never on subject alone. A subject is only unique within its issuer; two providers can hand you the same string. The link table's primary key is that pair, so two simultaneous first logins cannot both create a link.

Creating an account and linking it are one act. They run in one transaction, so a failed link takes the half-made account with it — otherwise every retry leaves another orphan beside the last one. The new account is then read back through the configured source before it signs in: what signs in has to be what the next request will load, and the source is what decides who may sign in at all.

A matching e-mail address is never a link. Not even a verified one: anybody who can get a provider to assert an address could then walk into the account that uses it. Attaching a second provider is a separate act, performed by somebody already signed in — and the person who finishes it must be the person who started it:

<a href="<?= route('oauth.connect', ['provider' => 'github']) ?>">Connect GitHub</a>

docs.title: Custom login integration
docs.text:
For application-owned routes, call oauth() to use the protocol flow directly. The start action and callback action are separate HTTP handlers. In the start action:

use function Naf\redirect;
use function Naf\OAuth\Client\oauth;

return redirect(oauth('google')->authorizationUrl());

In the callback action, after the provider redirects back:

use Naf\OAuth\Client\Token\Tokens;
use function Naf\app;
use function Naf\redirect;
use function Naf\Auth\auth;
use function Naf\OAuth\Client\oauth;

$callback = oauth('google')->callback();   // throws unless everything verifies
$external = $callback->identity;

$user = $yourAccounts->findBySubject($external->issuer, $external->subject)
    ?? throw new RuntimeException('Not linked.');

auth()->setIdentity($user, 'database');
if ($callback->token !== null) {
    app()->container()->get(Tokens::class)->remember($callback);
}

return redirect($callback->redirectTo);

These are handler fragments: $yourAccounts is your application's account lookup service, which finds the linked identity by issuer and subject, and 'database' must be a registered Auth provider able to reload that identity. Configure Google's callback URL to reach this callback handler. Handle rejected or unlinked accounts before completing sign-in.

remember() is an instance method on the container's Tokens service. Resolve it only when the callback carries a token: the default token-store binding throws when provider token storage is disabled. Call it only after successful sign-in. Do not retain credentials from a callback the application refuses to complete.

docs.title: Concurrent login attempts
docs.text: Logins are keyed by their own state, so a person with three tabs open finishes all three. Each entry is consumed on use and expires after ten minutes, which is also what makes a replayed callback fail.

docs.title: External identity data
docs.text:
Callback: identity, purpose (LOGIN or LINK), initiator, redirectTo, token.

ExternalIdentity: provider, issuer, subject, claims, and email / emailVerified / name for convenience. emailVerified is true only for a literal true — providers have sent "true", 1 and "1" there.

docs.title: Calling the provider afterwards
docs.text:
Local login needs no persistent provider token. Enable the following integration when the application must call the provider on the user's behalf after the sign-in request.

Store the required access and refresh tokens encrypted, request the API's scopes and check what the provider actually grants.

// app/config.php
'oauth' => [
    'tokens' => [
        'store' => true,
        'key'   => 'BASE64_OF_32_RANDOM_BYTES',
    ],
],

vendor/bin/naf oauth:doctor describes key generation. Keep the encryption key outside the database and source repository. Losing it makes stored grants unreadable and requires new consent from affected users.

Then, wherever the API call happens:

use function Naf\OAuth\Client\oauth;
use function Naf\OAuth\Client\oauth_token;
use function Naf\Auth\auth;
use function Naf\Client\client;
use function Naf\redirect;
use Nyholm\Psr7\Request;

$token = oauth_token('google');

if ($token === null || !$token->grants('https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly')) {
    return redirect(oauth('google')->grantUrl(
        ['https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly'],
        auth()->providerName(),
        (string) auth()->id(),
    ));
}

$response = client()->sendRequest(new Request(
    'GET',
    'https://www.googleapis.com/calendar/v3/calendars/primary/events',
    ['Authorization' => 'Bearer ' . $token->accessToken],
));

oauth_token() returns a usable token or null when no grant is available. Expired access tokens are refreshed and stored. Provider outages raise an exception; they do not imply that consent was withdrawn.

docs.title: Granted scopes
docs.text:
What the application may do is decided entirely by the scopes on the consent screen. Ask for nothing beyond openid email profile — the default — and there is no API access at all.

A provider may grant fewer scopes than requested. Inspect $token->scope and use $token->grants(...) before an API operation that needs a specific grant.

docs.title: Incremental consent
docs.text:
